Start with the failure, not the feature. The author's decision-tree post maps four failure modes to what survives them: an instance or node failure is absorbed by RAC without any role change; a site or region loss is survived only by an independent copy, which is Data Guard; block corruption is handled by Data Guard (the standby has its own writes, and Active Data Guard can repair blocks from the other side) and by validated backups; and human or logical error, the bad DELETE or dropped table, is survived by neither RAC nor Data Guard because both faithfully replicate the mistake. Only backups, point-in-time recovery and Flashback cover that row, so they are mandatory in every branch of the tree. Then apply the Azure target constraints. Azure Service Bus | service-bus | Azure Service Bus is a managed enterprise message broker with queues for point-to-point messaging and topics with filtered subscriptions for publish-subscribe. It offers sessions for FIFO and request-response, dead-letter subqueues, scheduled delivery, message deferral, duplicate detection, autoforwarding and transactions that group operations against a single entity. The wire protocol is AMQP 1.0 and Azure Functions, Logic Apps and Event Grid integrate natively. It is the closest Azure equivalent to Oracle Advanced Queuing for application-level messaging, with the important difference that the broker lives outside the database, so enqueue and dequeue are not part of a database transaction. | Basic, Standard and Premium tiers. Premium is fully JMS 2.0 compliant and supports zone-redundant namespaces; Standard supports the JMS 1.1 queue subset.

Create an empty CDB on the VM. Run AutoUpgrade with the non-CDB as source and the CDB as target to upgrade and plug in. Update connection strings to the PDB service name.

Trust none of the defaults. Profile the real values (unconstrained NUMBER has no dictionary bound, so sample the maximum precision and scale in the data), then pin an exact type explicitly: decimal(p,s) on Azure SQL, numeric(p,s) on PostgreSQL, or a true integer type only when the sample shows no fractions. In Ora2Pg that means overriding DEFAULT_NUMERIC or disabling PG_INTEGER_TYPE; in SSMA it means editing the Type Mapping page before Convert Schema. | Unconstrained NUMBER: float(53), bigint, or numeric? | Microsoft's SSMA default converts a NUMBER declared without precision or scale to float(53), a binary floating-point type that cannot hold most decimal fractions exactly. Ora2Pg's documented type table says the same column becomes numeric, yet its shipped defaults (PG_INTEGER_TYPE on, DEFAULT_NUMERIC bigint) make an out-of-the-box run emit bigint, which drops the fractional part entirely. Three tools' worth of guidance, three different answers for one declaration.

result:
**Verdict: The reference passages don't answer this.** None of them gives an IOPS figure for Premium SSD v2.

- **Passage [1]** is the only one that covers Oracle VM storage. It lists "Premium SSD, Ultra Disk, Azure NetApp Files" as storage options but gives no performance limits and doesn't mention Premium SSD v2 by name.
- **Passages [2] and [4]** mention disk metrics and throughput alert rules for monitoring. They say nothing about disk limits.
- **The other passages** are about Azure SQL Database, Service Bus, RAC vs. Data Guard, non-CDB conversion and NUMBER type mapping. None of them is relevant to this question.

You were strict about using only these passages, so I haven't filled in the number from memory. You can find it on Microsoft's managed disk types page (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/disks-types), in the Premium SSD v2 section. The IOPS a VM can actually reach is also capped by its own size limits, so check both.
